description: Two Pointers track: 4 lessons, 10 knowledge checks, 7 practice problems.

coding.title: Pair Sum in a Sorted Array
coding.problemStatement:
Given an array sorted in **non-decreasing** order and a target, find the two different positions `i < j` whose values add up to the target.

Exactly one such pair exists. Print `i` and `j` (0-based).

Try to use O(1) extra memory — no hash map needed, because the array is sorted.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n and target. The second line contains n integers in non-decreasing order.
coding.outputFormat: Two integers i and j with i < j and a[i] + a[j] = target.

coding.title: Count Pairs Below a Target
coding.problemStatement: Given an **unsorted** array and a target, count the pairs of positions `i < j` with `a[i] + a[j] < target`.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n and target. The second line contains n integers.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the number of pairs.

examples.explanation: (-1, 1), (-1, 2) and (-1, 1) — the second 1 is a different position — have sums below 2.

coding.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
coding.problemStatement:
Given an array sorted in non-decreasing order — which may contain negative numbers — print the square of every element, also in non-decreasing order.

Squaring and then sorting is O(n log n); the array is already sorted, so aim for O(n).
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. The second line contains n integers in non-decreasing order.
coding.outputFormat: n space-separated integers: the squares in non-decreasing order.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
result = [0] * n
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
for pos in range(n - 1, -1, -1):     # fill from the largest square down
    if abs(a[lo]) > abs(a[hi]):
        result[pos] = a[lo] * a[lo]
        lo += 1
    else:
        result[pos] = a[hi] * a[hi]
        hi -= 1
print(*result)

coding.title: Container With Most Water
coding.problemStatement:
There are n vertical lines; line `i` stands at position `i` with height `h[i]`. Any two lines, together with the ground, form a container. It holds `min(h[i], h[j]) * (j - i)` units of water.

Find the most water a single container can hold.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. The second line contains the n heights.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the maximum amount of water.

coding.title: Three Sum Closest
coding.problemStatement:
Given an array and a target, choose three elements at **different positions** whose sum is as close to the target as possible, and print that sum.

If two different sums are equally close (one above the target, one below), print the **smaller** one.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n and target. The second line contains n integers.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the closest sum.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
n, target = map(int, input().split())
a = sorted(map(int, input().split()))
best = a[0] + a[1] + a[2]
for i in range(n - 2):              # fix the first element
    lo, hi = i + 1, n - 1
    while lo < hi:                  # sweep the other two
        s = a[i] + a[lo] + a[hi]
        if (abs(s - target), s) < (abs(best - target), best):
            best = s
        if s < target:
            lo += 1
        elif s > target:
            hi -= 1
        else:
            break
print(best)

coding.title: Count Valid Triangles
coding.problemStatement: Given n stick lengths, count how many ways you can choose three sticks (at three different positions) that form a triangle with **positive area** — each side must be strictly shorter than the sum of the other two.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. The second line contains the n stick lengths.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the number of valid triples.

examples.explanation: (2, 3, 4) using the first 2, (2, 3, 4) using the second 2, and (2, 2, 3). (2, 2, 4) is flat: 2 + 2 is not more than 4.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
n = int(input())
a = sorted(map(int, input().split()))
count = 0
for k in range(n - 1, 1, -1):     # a[k] is the longest side
    lo, hi = 0, k - 1
    while lo < hi:
        if a[lo] + a[hi] > a[k]:
            count += hi - lo        # every index in [lo, hi) also works with hi
            hi -= 1
        else:
            lo += 1
print(count)

coding.title: Sort Colors
coding.problemStatement:
An array holds only the values 0, 1 and 2 (red, white and blue). Rearrange it so all 0s come first, then all 1s, then all 2s, and print it.

The classic challenge: do it in **one pass** with O(1) extra memory — no library sort and no counting pass.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. The second line contains n values, each 0, 1 or 2.
coding.outputFormat: The n values in sorted order, space-separated.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
low, mid, high = 0, 0, n - 1
# a[:low] are 0s, a[low:mid] are 1s, a[mid:high+1] unknown, a[high+1:] are 2s
while mid <= high:
    if a[mid] == 0:
        a[low], a[mid] = a[mid], a[low]
        low += 1
        mid += 1
    elif a[mid] == 1:
        mid += 1
    else:
        a[mid], a[high] = a[high], a[mid]
        high -= 1          # don't advance mid: the swapped-in value is unexamined
print(*a)

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: why moving lo is safe
mcqs.questionText: Searching a sorted array for a pair with sum `target`, you find `a[lo] + a[hi] < target` and move `lo` one step right. Why can no answer be lost?
mcqs.explanation: Every partner still available to a[lo] sits at index hi or lower, so it is at most a[hi]. If even the largest one is too small, a[lo] belongs to no valid pair — discarding it is safe. The same argument, mirrored, justifies moving hi when the sum is too big.

options.optionText: a[lo] plus any element at or before hi is at most a[lo] + a[hi], which is already too small
Because the array has no duplicates
Because hi will come back to check a[lo] later
It can lose answers; you must also try moving hi

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: tracing the pointers
Two Pointers check: counting many pairs at once
mcqs.questionText: Counting pairs with sum below `target` in a sorted array: `a[lo] + a[hi] < target`. How many pairs does that single check prove?
mcqs.explanation: Every element between lo + 1 and hi is at most a[hi], so a[lo] plus any of them is also below target. Add hi − lo at once and move lo — the whole count takes O(n) after sorting, instead of checking all n²/2 pairs.

options.optionText: hi - lo: a[lo] with every index from lo + 1 to hi
Exactly one: (lo, hi)
lo + 1
n - hi

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: which side to move
mcqs.questionText: In Container With Most Water, h[lo] = 3 and h[hi] = 8. Why move lo rather than hi?
mcqs.explanation: With lo fixed, every other partner is closer, so the width shrinks, and the height can never exceed h[lo] = 3. So line lo has already had its best container — drop it. Moving hi instead could skip the true answer.

options.optionText: Any narrower container that keeps line lo is capped at height 3 and is narrower, so it can't beat the current one
Moving the taller side always lowers the height
lo is always moved first by convention
Either works; the answer is the same

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: running the squeeze
mcqs.explanation: The best pair is heights 8 (index 1) and 7 (index 8): min(8, 7) × 7 = 49. The squeeze reaches it in n − 1 steps without trying all 36 pairs.

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: where the largest square is
mcqs.questionText: In a sorted array that contains negative numbers, like `[-9, -2, 0, 3, 7]`, where is the element with the largest square?
mcqs.explanation: Squares grow with distance from 0, and the elements farthest from 0 are at the ends: the most negative on the left, the most positive on the right. So compare the two ends, place the larger square at the back of the result, and move that pointer inward.

options.optionText: At one of the two ends
Always at the right end
In the middle, near 0
Anywhere — you must scan

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: cost of fixing one element
mcqs.questionText: For each element in turn you fix it, then run an O(n) two-pointer sweep over the rest of the sorted array. What is the total time, including the sort?
mcqs.explanation: n fixed elements × an O(n) sweep = O(n²), and the O(n log n) sort is smaller. That beats the O(n³) of checking every triple.

options.optionText: O(n²)
O(n log n)
O(n³)
O(n)

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: counting triangles in bulk
mcqs.questionText: Sticks are sorted and `a[k]` is the longest side. With `a[lo] + a[hi] > a[k]` (and lo < hi < k), how many valid triangles with sides hi and k does that prove?
mcqs.explanation: Every index i between lo and hi − 1 has a[i] >= a[lo], so a[i] + a[hi] > a[k] too, and the other two triangle inequalities hold automatically because a[k] is the longest side. Count them all, then move hi down.

options.optionText: hi - lo: every index from lo to hi - 1 works with hi and k
Just one
k - hi
lo + 1

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: the regions of the flag
mcqs.questionText: In the one-pass Dutch national flag algorithm, what does the part of the array between `mid` and `high` hold?
mcqs.explanation: The pointers split the array into four regions: 0s before low, 1s from low to mid − 1, unexamined values from mid to high, and 2s after high. Each step examines a[mid] and shrinks the unexamined region by one.

options.optionText: Values not examined yet
Only 1s
Only 2s
Values that are already in their final place

mcqs.title: Two Pointers check: after swapping with high
mcqs.questionText: When `a[mid]` is 2, you swap it with `a[high]` and decrease `high`. Why must `mid` stay where it is?
mcqs.explanation: a[high] could be a 0, 1 or 2. Advancing mid would leave it unclassified — a 0 would stay stuck in the middle. When swapping with low, advancing is safe, because the value from low is already known to be a 1 (or it is the same element).

options.optionText: The value swapped into a[mid] came from the unexamined region and hasn't been looked at yet
Because a[mid] is now guaranteed to be 1
To avoid reading past the end of the array
It doesn't matter; advancing mid is also correct

lessons.title: Pointers from both ends of a sorted array
lessons.summary: Start at the smallest and largest values; each comparison safely discards one of them — O(n) instead of checking every pair.
objectives: Find a pair with a given sum in a sorted array with two pointers and O(1) memory
Explain why moving a pointer can never skip an answer
Count pairs that satisfy a condition in bulk rather than one at a time
lessons.concept:
The Arrays track used two pointers moving the **same** way — a read and a write pointer, or one pointer per array. A second family starts the pointers at **opposite ends** and moves them toward each other.

Looking for two values in a sorted array that sum to `target`:

```python
lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
while lo < hi:
    s = a[lo] + a[hi]
    if s == target:
        return lo, hi
    if s < target:
        lo += 1      # need a bigger sum
    else:
        hi -= 1      # need a smaller sum
```

## Why it's correct

When the sum is too small, pair `a[lo]` with anything still available: the largest partner left is `a[hi]`, and even that is not enough. So `a[lo]` is in **no** valid pair — throw it away. The mirrored argument throws away `a[hi]` when the sum is too big. Each step discards one element for good, so there are at most n − 1 steps: **O(n) time, O(1) memory** — no hash map needed.

## Counting pairs in bulk

The same argument can count. If `a[lo] + a[hi] < target`, then `a[lo]` plus *any* element from `lo + 1` to `hi` is also below target — that's `hi - lo` pairs proven by a single comparison. Add them, move `lo`, and the count takes O(n) after an O(n log n) sort.

Sorting destroys the original positions, so this works for questions about **values** or **counts**. If you need original indices from unsorted input, sort `(value, index)` pairs, or use the hash-map approach from the Hashing track.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Using opposite-end pointers on unsorted data.** The "too small, so discard `a[lo]`" argument depends on the order.
- **`while lo <= hi`.** When `lo == hi` you'd pair an element with itself.
- **Counting one pair per step.** When a check proves a whole range, add the whole range (`hi - lo`).
- **`int` overflow** when counting pairs in C++/Java: n = 10⁵ gives up to 5 × 10⁹ pairs — use `long long`/`long`.
practice: Pair Sum in a Sorted Array

lessons.title: Squeezing: moving the pointer that can't do better
lessons.summary: When the answer depends on both ends, move the one that has already had its best chance.
objectives: Solve Container With Most Water in O(n) by always moving the shorter side
Build a sorted result from both ends of a sorted array
Justify a pointer move by arguing that the discarded element can't improve the answer
lessons.concept:
Opposite-end pointers work for more than sums. The general rule: **at each step, find the end that can no longer be part of a better answer, and discard it.**

## Container With Most Water

Two lines at `lo` and `hi` hold `min(h[lo], h[hi]) × (hi − lo)` units of water. Start with the widest container, lines 0 and n − 1. Suppose `h[lo]` is the shorter one. Any other container that uses line `lo` is **narrower**, and its height can't exceed `h[lo]` — so it holds less. Line `lo` has had its best container already: move `lo` inward.

```python
lo, hi, best = 0, len(h) - 1, 0
while lo < hi:
    best = max(best, min(h[lo], h[hi]) * (hi - lo))
    if h[lo] < h[hi]:
        lo += 1
    else:
        hi -= 1
```

Moving the **taller** side instead would be wrong: the next container might be taller and worth more, yet you'd have given up the line that could reach it.

## Building from both ends

Squaring a sorted array with negatives (`[-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]`) scrambles the order — but the **largest** square is always at one of the ends, since those are the values farthest from 0. So fill the result from the back: compare the two ends, write the bigger square at the last free position, move that pointer in. O(n), no sort.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Moving the taller line** in Container With Most Water — it can skip the best container.
- **Filling the squares from the front.** The *smallest* square can be anywhere in the middle; only the largest is guaranteed to be at an end.
- **Stopping at `lo < hi` when every element must be placed.** When filling a result, loop over all n positions (the last element has `lo == hi`).
- **Not writing down why a move is safe.** If you can't say why the discarded end can't do better, the greedy move is probably wrong.

lessons.title: Fix one, sweep two: triples in O(n²)
lessons.summary: For problems about three elements, fix the first with a loop and solve the remaining pair with two pointers.
objectives: Reduce a three-element problem to n two-pointer problems
Track the closest sum with a clear tie-break
Count triangles by fixing the longest side
lessons.concept:
Checking every triple is O(n³). If the array is sorted, you can do better: **fix one element with a loop, and find the other two with a two-pointer sweep** over the rest. That is n sweeps of O(n) each — **O(n²)**.

## Three Sum Closest

For each `i`, sweep `lo = i + 1` and `hi = n − 1`. Compare each sum with the best so far; then, like the pair search, move `lo` if the sum is too small and `hi` if it's too big. An exact hit can't be beaten, so stop.

```python
a.sort()
best = a[0] + a[1] + a[2]
for i in range(n - 2):
    lo, hi = i + 1, n - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = a[i] + a[lo] + a[hi]
        if (abs(s - target), s) < (abs(best - target), best):
            best = s          # closer — or equally close but smaller
        if s < target:
            lo += 1
        elif s > target:
            hi -= 1
        else:
            return s
```

Comparing the tuple `(distance, sum)` builds the tie-break ("prefer the smaller sum") into one comparison.

## Choosing what to fix

For **triangles**, fix the **longest** side `a[k]`. After sorting, the only inequality that can fail is `a[i] + a[j] > a[k]` — the other two hold automatically. Then sweep `lo = 0`, `hi = k − 1`: whenever `a[lo] + a[hi] > a[k]`, every index from `lo` to `hi − 1` also works with `hi`, so add `hi − lo` and move `hi` down.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Forgetting to sort** — every pointer move relies on it.
- **Restarting `lo` at 0 for Three Sum Closest.** Start at `i + 1` so each element is used once and each triple is seen once.
- **Fixing the wrong element for triangles.** Fix the longest side; fixing the shortest leaves two inequalities to check.
- **Using `>=` for triangles.** `2 + 2 = 4` makes a flat "triangle" with zero area; the inequality must be strict.

lessons.title: Partitioning in place: the Dutch national flag
lessons.summary: Three pointers split the array into regions and sort three kinds of values in a single pass.
objectives: Maintain several regions of an array with pointers and an invariant
Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass with O(1) memory
Know when to advance a pointer after a swap, and when not to
lessons.concept:
Some problems need the array **rearranged into groups**: negatives before positives, values below a pivot before values above it, or three colours in order. Pointers can maintain those groups in place.

The **Dutch national flag** algorithm sorts an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass. Three pointers split it into four regions:

| indices | holds |
|---|---|
| `0 … low − 1` | 0s |
| `low … mid − 1` | 1s |
| `mid … high` | not examined yet |
| `high + 1 … n − 1` | 2s |

At first everything is unexamined (`low = mid = 0`, `high = n − 1`). Each step looks at `a[mid]`:

- **0**: swap it into the 0s region (`a[low]`), then advance both `low` and `mid`.
- **1**: it's already in the right region — advance `mid`.
- **2**: swap it with `a[high]` and shrink the 2s boundary (`high -= 1`). **Don't advance `mid`**: the value that just arrived came from the unexamined region.

The loop ends when the unexamined region is empty (`mid > high`). Every step shrinks it by one, so the whole thing is one pass: O(n) time, O(1) memory.

## Why not just count?

For plain 0/1/2 values, counting them and rewriting also works in two passes. The flag algorithm matters when the items are **records** with a 3-way key (low / medium / high priority): you move the real items, and it's the same partition step quicksort uses around a pivot.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Advancing `mid` after swapping with `high`.** The incoming value is unexamined; a 0 would be left stranded among the 1s.
- **`while mid < high`.** The element at `mid == high` still needs to be examined.
- **Losing track of the regions.** Write the invariant (what each range holds) as a comment before coding; every branch must keep it true.
